newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: ABB CEO says Q1 orders were good.
newsitem.headline: ABB CEO says Q1 orders were good.

text.p: Goran Lindahl, chief executive and president of electrical engineering group ABB Asea Brown Boveri AG, said first quarter orders came in slightly better than expected due to the booking of several large projects.

Lindahl also said in an interview with Reuters Financial Television that business so far this year was developing according to plans, but overall 1997 would be a rather flat year due to the second year of slowdown in Western Europe.
"We are basically following our plans," Lindahl said, referring to ABB's first quarter results announced on April 22.
"There were no surprises, but maybe I can say that on the order side I was surprised they were slightly better than expected, driven by a number of large projects."
In the first quarter of 1997 ABB's net profit rose eight percent to $236 million, while orders rose 22 percent to $10,076 million.

Although Lindahl expects ABB's earnings in the long run to become less dependant on business cycles, ABB's performance in 1997 will still reflect the recent pattern where three years of earnings growth are followed by two years of flat earnings.
Asked why Lindahl's earnings forecast for 1997 was so cautious, he said the second year of a downturn is worse than the first year and he saw no reason for why that should be different this year.
Lindahl confirmed that ABB's forecast for 1997 is that net income will at least reach the 1996 level.
In 1996 ABB's group net profit rose 16 percent on a comparable basis to $1,233 million.
"I foresee for the future that we will be less and less dependant on business cycles," Lindahl said.
First of all ABB restructures to curb the effect of fluctuating demand and secondly because of the move to low-cost emerging markets where there is no decline, but only growth.
"The more we have (in emerging markets) the less dependant we are on cycles.
The third reason is that ABB increasingly outsources components.
"If you add all this together, then you will see over time that we become less dependant on cycles," he said.
Over the last nine years, ABB's earnings have shown two distinct growth phases and one phase of stagnation. In 1996 there was a slowdown in the earnings growth rate.
"What is good with ABB is the diversity in products and systems and different cycles. We very seldom have a tremendous downturn, but have a flattening, a stagnation in our growth," Lindahl said.
